notes: The ward's ten questions, transcribed from docs/design/CHARGEN-DAGGERFALL-DRAFT.md section 3. Voice per the approved sample: second person, concrete Trojian nouns, past-defining moral dilemmas, three defensible answers each carrying its own rationale clause, each scoring exactly one axis. The axes are the approved Option 1 trio -- the ward's three childhoods. Tie for dominant (section 3.3): the tied axis the player's last-question answer scored wins; if that answer scored the third axis, fixed order A > B > C. Answer order is shuffled per question at DISPLAY time only -- Daggerfall's own guard against pattern-marking; the authored order here is always A, B, C. The owner line-edits the doc; a sync pass moves his edits here.

questions.prompt: Quarter-day. Your family's ground penny is short by three Royals and the Den Duke's man is at the gate. What do you do?

answers.text: You meet him at the gate and say it plain: the penny is short, and your hands will make up the difference. A debt owned out loud is half worked off.
You take the roofs to the strand. The tide is out, and three Royals of wrack lies on the mud for whoever beats the gulls to it.
You fetch the household's rent-book and walk it to the Mission. The arrears are wrong by the roll's own arithmetic, and a priest will weigh a page over a fist.

questions.prompt: The crane gang's boss pays you a child's wage for a hand's work, and you both know it. What do you do?

answers.text: You put down the hook and tell him so, in front of the gang. A wage argued in the open stays argued.
You take the wage and learn which nights the tally-clerk leaves early. Knowing a yard's habits is worth more than a day's difference.
You count the crates yourself for a week, then show him his own tally. A boss cheats a child who cannot add.

questions.prompt: An older Gullet tough has taken your basket at the Bottom link every dusk this quarter. What do you do?

answers.text: You stand once and take the beating that comes with keeping it. He needs to win every dusk; you only need to cost him one.
You go home a different way each night. The Gullet has more roofs than he has evenings.
You ask Gullet Mag what he answers to. Every tough in the Gullet pays respects to someone, and respects can be spoken to.

questions.prompt: Old Cobb's best rat-dog slipped its cage and hangs snagged in the outfall grate. The tide is rising. What do you do?

answers.text: You wade in and take her out now. Cold water forgives the quick and drowns the careful.
You use what you know. The grate lifts on a pin the mudlarks keep quiet, and the tide gives you until the turn. So does the dog.
You run for Cobb. A dog in a panic bites its rescuer, it will let its own man touch it, and you know exactly where he drinks.

questions.prompt: Brann's counter-hand miscounts your mother's change, a half-Royal in your favor, and nobody sees it. What do you do?

answers.text: You hand it back across the counter before you have decided anything. What is done in the open cannot be held against you.
You keep it. The counter has kept plenty of yours, and the sea does not hand things back either.
You return it quietly at shutter-time. A chandler who trusts your family's tally will carry them through a lean quarter, and lean quarters come.

questions.prompt: Pay-night at the Bilge. Your father is drunk with the packet on him and a crimp works the room. What do you do?

answers.text: You walk in and carry him home yourself, past whoever objects. Let the room watch.
You wait in the arcade shadow until the crimp picks his man, and you make sure it is not your father. Out the back, before anyone chooses him.
You pay Redda's hand a copper to bunk him upstairs till morning. The Bilge keeps what it is paid to keep, and a copper is cheaper than a wage.

questions.prompt: The Watch nails a warrant to the notice board naming a Rows lodger you know was at sea that night. What do you do?

answers.text: You climb the Rise and tell the sergeant his paper is wrong, and you give your name when he asks for it.
You say nothing to the post. Word can cross the roofs and meet the man's ship before the Watch meets the berth.
You copy the warrant's dates and walk them against the Weighhouse berth ledger. Paper argues best with paper.

questions.prompt: A hungry quarter, and the Mission's soup line is long. A bigger kid shoves in ahead of a smaller one. What do you do?

answers.text: You put him back where he was. A line only works if someone is willing to hold it.
You leave the line to those who cannot do otherwise. The strand feeds whoever works the low water, and the tide is out.
You take the ladle end and serve. The last bowl always finds the one who served, and the priest's eye finds them too.

questions.prompt: A heavy purse lies by the crawl-gap on the roof-decks. It is not yours, and nobody is asking after it. What do you do?

answers.text: You call "whose is this?" down the deck and hold it up. A thing done in the open cannot be made into something else later.
You leave it exactly where it lies and remember who comes back for it. Roof-money goes to whoever asks after it least, and what crosses the roofs is worth more than the weight.
You carry it to Gullet Mag and let the ruin's gray voice judge. A favor with the judge outlasts any purse.

questions.prompt: At black tide you see a hull berth with no lights and no bell. By morning everyone says no ship came in. What do you do?

answers.text: You tell the Watch at first bell, and you stand by it when they ask how you know.
You say nothing, and you are on the quay, unseen, at the next black tide.
You mark what you could read of her name and look for it in the Weighhouse's posted list. A ship that is not on the list is a fact worth keeping.
